title: The Man Who Was Supposed to Be Dead
subtitle: After Always · Chapter 1 of 40
content:
The first thing Professor McGonagall told me when I arrived at Hogwarts was that the castle had survived.

The second was that Severus Snape had, too.

I thought I had misheard her.

Rain struck the high windows of the entrance hall in pale sheets, and half the ceiling still wore scaffolding where curses had split stone during the battle. Portraits leaned against walls awaiting repair. A suit of armor had been stacked in pieces beside the staircase with a handwritten sign that read DO NOT REASSEMBLE WITHOUT PROFESSOR FLITWICK.

“Professor Snape,” I repeated.

McGonagall's mouth became a thin line. “Mr. Snape, at present. His professional status is a matter the Board will eventually decide, assuming the Ministry does not make a greater nuisance of itself first.”

I tightened my grip on the handle of my case. I had been hired to audit the Potions stores, identify contamination, recover anything useful, and make certain the school did not reopen with cursed ingredients sitting beside first-year cauldrons. That had sounded difficult enough when the letter arrived.

Nobody had mentioned sharing a dungeon with a dead man.

“How?” I asked.

“Stubbornness,” McGonagall said. “And preparation. Apparently he had been taking a broad-spectrum antivenom for weeks before the battle. Madam Pomfrey says it should not have been sufficient. Mr. Snape says Madam Pomfrey has always underestimated the importance of dosage.”

That sounded more like a living person than a legend.

McGonagall looked at me over the rims of her spectacles. “He will dislike you.”

“Is that part of the contract?”

“No. Merely a courtesy.”

I almost smiled.

She did not.

The descent into the dungeons was colder than I remembered from my own school years. I had not attended Hogwarts, but every British magical child knew its stories, and every potioneer knew the shape of the place through professional gossip. Snape's classroom. Snape's stores. Snape's impossible standards. Snape's temper.

Snape's body in the Shrieking Shack, according to the newspapers.

The door to the Potions classroom stood open.

Inside, broken stools had been stacked against one wall. Several worktables bore scorch marks. A cauldron had melted into a blackened puddle of pewter near the back of the room. Shelves stood half-empty, their jars sealed with Ministry evidence wax.

A man in black robes was standing on a ladder with one hand braced against the stone.

He was thinner than the photographs. That was my first thought.

My second was that he had no business being on a ladder.

A pale scar disappeared beneath the high collar wrapped around his throat. Another marked the edge of his jaw. His hair fell to his shoulders, black and uneven where it had been cut away during treatment. He was reaching for a jar on the top shelf with the slow precision of someone who did not trust his balance and would sooner fall to his death than admit it.

“Professor Snape?”

His hand stopped.

He turned his head.

Black eyes moved over me, then my case, then the clipboard tucked under my arm.

“No.”

I waited.

He descended one rung.

“Professor Snape is, according to three newspapers, two Ministry memoranda, and an especially enthusiastic obituary in the Daily Prophet, dead.” His voice was low and rough, more damaged than dramatic. “You may address the inconvenience before you as Snape.”

“McGonagall called you Mr. Snape.”

“Minerva is experimenting with optimism.”

He stepped down another rung. His foot slipped.

I crossed the room before I could think better of it and caught the ladder.

His gaze dropped to my hands.

“I had it.”

“I noticed.”

“You were under the impression that catching a stationary ladder constitutes heroism?”

“No. I was under the impression that paperwork is worse when the subject dies during the audit.”

For one beat, nothing happened.

Then the corner of his mouth moved.

Not a smile. More the memory of one.

He climbed down.

“I assume you are the contractor Minerva insisted upon inflicting on my stores.”

“I prefer independent potioneer.”

“I prefer competent people. We shall both endure disappointment.”

That one made me smile outright.

He looked faintly offended by the success of his own insult.

I set my case on the nearest intact table. “My job is to inventory what survived, identify anything cursed or adulterated, and separate school stock from materials the Ministry may claim as evidence.”

“My job, apparently, is to prevent you from throwing away anything valuable because a label frightens you.”

“I brought dragon-hide gloves.”

“How reassuring.”

“And I can read Latin.”

“A triumph of modern education.”

“And handwriting.”

His expression changed.

Only slightly.

It was enough.

I opened my case and removed a stack of blank tags, a silver testing spoon, three self-inking quills, and a narrow brass instrument for measuring residual spellwork. “If you have private research notes among the school materials, identify them. I have no interest in stealing your work.”

“Everyone has an interest in stealing useful work.”

“Then I have no interest in being caught.”

Again, that almost-smile.

He turned away before it could become anything else.

We began with the west wall.

The first hour taught me three things.

Snape could identify an ingredient by scent from six feet away.

He considered alphabetical organization evidence of moral weakness.

And pain made him vicious.

The first time his left hand began to tremble, he tucked it into his sleeve and accused me of misclassifying powdered moonstone. The second time, he sat down without comment and made me bring each jar to him. By the third, I understood the pattern.

I did not mention it.

That seemed to surprise him more than concern would have.

“Boomslang skin,” I said, holding up a sealed jar.

“Contaminated.”

“The wax is intact.”

“The contents are gray.”

“They're dried.”

“They are gray.”

I looked more closely.

He was right. The scales had a dull, powdery cast that I might have missed under the dungeon lamps.

“What happened?”

“Storage charm failure. Possibly intentional.”

“Carrows?”

His face closed.

“Possibly.”

I marked the jar for destruction.

Several shelves later, my instrument gave a sharp chime over a crate of lacewing flies.

Snape straightened in his chair.

“What?”

“Residual compulsion.”

His eyes sharpened. “Show me.”

I passed him the instrument instead of the crate.

He stared at me.

“You do not hand unknown cursed material to someone recovering from nerve damage,” I said.

“I am aware of basic laboratory procedure.”

“Good. Then we agree.”

He looked as though agreement physically pained him.

I opened the crate with my wand from across the table.

The scent that rose from it was sweet and metallic.

Snape went still.

“Do not breathe that.”

I sealed my mouth and nose with a bubble charm. He did the same. Together, we leaned over the open crate.

Beneath the lacewing flies lay six narrow glass phials, each wrapped in black cloth.

Snape's face lost what little color it had.

“You know them,” I said.

He did not answer.

His fingers had closed around the edge of the table.

“Snape.”

“I brewed them.”

The words were barely audible through the charm.

“For whom?”

His eyes met mine.

“Voldemort.”

The dungeon seemed to become colder.

I had expected spoiled roots. Cursed jars. Maybe a few illegal ingredients hidden in a locked cabinet.

I had not expected evidence.

Snape stood too quickly. The room tilted under him; I saw it happen in the sudden tightening of his jaw. He reached for the table and missed.

This time I caught his arm.

His body went rigid.

“Let go.”

“When you're steady.”

“I said—”

“And I heard you.”

We remained like that for two breaths. Then three.

His sleeve was cool beneath my hand. His arm was frighteningly thin.

At last, his balance returned.

I released him immediately.

He looked at the place where I had touched him as if it had become another piece of evidence.

“What do the phials do?” I asked.

His gaze returned to the crate.

“Nothing,” he said.

“That is rarely a useful property in a potion.”

“They were supposed to do something.”

I waited.

Snape's mouth twisted.

“I made certain they did not.”

Outside the narrow windows, thunder rolled somewhere over the grounds.

I looked down at the six phials hidden beneath the flies.

The audit had been underway for less than two hours.

Already, I knew I would not be leaving Hogwarts on schedule.
